title: Insurance Company Reviews: Is [Brand] Insurance Legit? A Practical Guide to Vetting Any Insurer
description: A step-by-step method for checking whether any insurance company, MGA, agency, or quote site is legitimate before you pay a premium or trust it with a claim.
author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: "Legit" doesn't mean one thing: carriers, MGAs, independent agencies, and lead-generation marketplaces all turn up in "is X insurance legit" searches, and each carries a different kind of risk.
Almost any US insurer or agent can be checked in under two minutes using your state Department of Insurance's license lookup and the NAIC's consumer information tools.

A company can be fully legitimate and still be a poor fit for you — ["admitted,"](/glossary/admitted-insurer) ["surplus lines,"](/glossary/surplus-lines-insurance) and ["MGA"](/glossary/managing-general-agent) describe how a policy is backed, not whether the company treats claims fairly.

[Financial strength ratings](/glossary/am-best-rating) from AM Best or S&P tell you whether an insurer can pay claims; the [NAIC complaint index](/glossary/naic-complaint-index) and patterns across review sites tell you whether it tends to pay them without a fight.

Generic or catchy-sounding names — things like "Insure 90" or "Smart Auto Insurance" — are frequently used by several unrelated small agencies at once, so match the exact legal name, license number, and underwriting carrier before you buy, not just the brand name.

faqs.question: How do I check if an insurance company is licensed in my state?
faqs.answer: Search the company's exact legal name (not just its marketing brand) on your state Department of Insurance's producer or company lookup tool, or on the NAIC's consumer information site. A licensed insurer will show an active status along with a company or NAIC code you can cross-check against your policy documents. External lookup: [NAIC consumer information site](https://content.naic.org/consumer-insurance).

faqs.question: What does it mean if an insurer is 'non-admitted' or 'surplus lines'?
faqs.answer: A [non-admitted, or surplus lines,](/glossary/surplus-lines-insurance) insurer is not licensed in your state and isn't bound by that state's standard rate filings or backed by its guaranty fund if it becomes insolvent. This is common and legal for hard-to-place risks, such as wildfire-zone homes — see [how this plays out for Bamboo Insurance's California policies](/qa/is-bamboo-insurance-admitted-in-california) — but it means you're taking on more of the financial-strength risk yourself, so checking the carrier's rating matters even more.

faqs.question: Is a cheap quote from an unfamiliar insurance company automatically a scam?
faqs.answer: No. Many legitimate regional insurers, MGAs, and specialty carriers are unfamiliar simply because they don't advertise nationally, the same way [NYCM](/qa/is-nycm-a-good-insurance-company) is a household name in New York but unknown everywhere else. A low price becomes a red flag only when it's paired with missing licensing information, pressure to pay in gift cards or crypto, or no verifiable underwriting carrier, similar to the vague marketing pages discussed in [our look at the confusing "Insure 90" search term](/qa/is-insure-90-legit) — not because the name is unfamiliar on its own.

content.text: Type almost any insurance brand into a search bar and Google will finish the sentence for you: "is [company] legit," "is [company] going out of business," "is [company] a scam." That instinct is a healthy one. Insurance is a promise to pay in the future, made in exchange for money now, and the market is crowded with carriers, agencies, managing general agents (MGAs), and quote-comparison sites that all use similar-sounding names. Some of those names belong to century-old mutual insurers. Others belong to a two-person marketing shop that has never underwritten a policy in its life. This guide walks through the exact checks that regulators, claims adjusters, and experienced agents use to tell the difference — and then applies them to eighteen real companies that show up constantly in these searches, each covered in a linked, in-depth answer below.
Why So Many Insurance Names Sound the Same

Before you can judge whether a company is legitimate, it helps to know what kind of company you're actually looking at. "Insurance" in a business name can describe four very different roles, and they carry very different levels of risk if something goes wrong, a distinction covered in more depth in [Agent vs. Broker vs. Insurer: Who Works for Whom?](/learn/agent-vs-broker-vs-insurer) and [What Is an Insurer? Carriers, Solvency, and Financial Strength Ratings](/learn/what-is-an-insurer).

headers: Who is on the hook for your claim
rows: Issues and underwrites the policy itself
The carrier's own balance sheet and reinsurance program
Underwrites, prices, and administers policies on behalf of one or more carriers, using delegated authority
The carrier(s) the MGA is authorized to bind — not the MGA itself

Independent agency or storefront (many businesses using generic names like ["Amigo Insurance"](/qa/is-amigo-insurance-legit) or ["Smart Auto Insurance"](/qa/smart-auto-insurance), or regional multi-carrier shops like [Amtex Insurance](/qa/amtex-auto-insurance) and [Able Insurance Agency](/qa/able-auto-insurance))
Sells and services policies from several carriers; does not set rates or hold claim reserves
Whichever carrier's name actually appears on your declarations page
Collects your information and sells it to agents and carriers who then contact you with quotes
No one — it is a marketing platform, not an insurer, and it never pays a claim

content.text: None of these four categories is inherently untrustworthy. But "is X insurance legit" needs a different answer depending on which category X falls into, which is why the checklist below asks you to identify the type of company first, including whether you're dealing with a [managing general agent (MGA)](/glossary/managing-general-agent) rather than the carrier itself. If you've landed here from a search about a confusingly generic brand name, [Insure 90](/qa/is-insure-90-legit) is a good example of just how tangled that can get.

items: Confirm licensing with your state's Department of Insurance producer or company search, or the NAIC's consumer information tools. A real US insurer or agent has an active license tied to its exact legal entity name, verifiable through the [NAIC's consumer information tools](https://content.naic.org/consumer-insurance), — not just a trade name or website domain, which is exactly the problem with a generic name like ["Amigo Insurance"](/qa/is-amigo-insurance-legit).

Check [admitted](/glossary/admitted-insurer) vs. [surplus lines (non-admitted)](/glossary/surplus-lines-insurance) status. Admitted carriers are bound by state rate filings and back the state guaranty fund if they fail; surplus lines carriers aren't. Being non-admitted isn't a scam — it's how many wildfire-, coastal-, and high-risk-zone policies get written, as [Bamboo Insurance's California book](/qa/is-bamboo-insurance-admitted-in-california) and [Slide Insurance's entry into California](/qa/is-slide-insurance-going-out-of-business) both show — but you should know which one you're buying.

Pull the company's [AM Best financial strength rating](/glossary/am-best-rating), or S&P/Moody's if AM Best doesn't rate it — lookup available directly at [ambest.com](https://web.ambest.com/ratings/default.aspx). A rating of B+ or better is generally considered adequate to pay claims; anything lower, or "not rated," deserves a closer look before you commit. [NYCM](/qa/is-nycm-a-good-insurance-company) and [Essentia](/qa/is-essentia-insurance-legit) are both good examples of insurers whose strong ratings are a real, checkable part of the story.

Read the [NAIC complaint index](/glossary/naic-complaint-index) under the exact legal company name, not the marketing name. A score meaningfully above 1.0 means the insurer draws more complaints than the industry average for its size and line of business — [NYCM's favorable complaint index](/qa/is-nycm-a-good-insurance-company) is one reason it consistently ranks well.

Cross-reference at least two independent review sources — the Better Business Bureau, Trustpilot, and your state's own complaint portal all publish different slices of the same picture. Be skeptical of reviews that arrive in a sudden cluster or repeat oddly similar phrasing; that pattern is a known sign of incentivized or fabricated reviews, and it's also why a [lead-generation marketplace like QuoteLab](/qa/what-is-quotelab) is worth reading about before you submit your information anywhere.

content.title: Red Flags That Apply Regardless of Company Size
content.text: Be cautious of any insurer or agent that pressures you to pay by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency; can't provide a fixed US business address or a named, licensed agent; issues a policy document with no NAIC company code printed on it; or promises guaranteed acceptance in a way that conflicts with your state's underwriting rules. Any one of these is reason enough to verify licensing before paying.
Brand Confusion: One Name, Several Unrelated Companies

A meaningful share of "is X legit" searches aren't actually about one company at all. Names like ["Insure 90"](/qa/is-insure-90-legit), ["Amigo Insurance"](/qa/is-amigo-insurance-legit), ["Smart Auto Insurance"](/qa/smart-auto-insurance), and ["Accusure Insurance"](/qa/accusure-insurance) are generic enough that they get reused by multiple unrelated local agencies, legacy software products, or long-closed businesses across different states — sometimes alongside completely unrelated content, like coinsurance terminology that happens to share the same numbers. Searching a brand name alone can point you to the wrong entity entirely, and the same caution applies to quote-comparison sites: a marketplace like [QuoteLab](/qa/what-is-quotelab) is legitimate but is not itself an insurer, which is easy to miss if you don't read past the headline. This is also worth understanding through the lens of an [independent agency vs. a managing general agent](/glossary/managing-general-agent) vs. a carrier — see [Independent vs. Captive Insurance Agencies](/qa/insurance-agencies-near-me-independent-vs-captive) for more on how agencies themselves are structured. The fix is always the same: match the exact business name, physical address, and license number on your quote or policy documents against your state's official lookup, rather than trusting the name on a search result or an ad.

Each of the following companies is one of the most-searched "is it legit" queries in the insurance-basics space. A short summary is below; the full, sourced answer for each is linked and covers licensing, financial ratings, and what a real customer should expect.

items: Slide Insurance — a publicly traded (NASDAQ: SLDE), Florida-based homeowners insurer that is actively expanding, not shutting down. See [Is Slide Insurance going out of business?](/qa/is-slide-insurance-going-out-of-business)

Bamboo Insurance — a California-focused managing general agent that places wildfire-zone homeowners coverage through a mix of admitted and surplus-lines carrier partners. See [Is Bamboo Insurance admitted in California?](/qa/is-bamboo-insurance-admitted-in-california)
NYCM (New York Central Mutual) — a New York-only mutual insurer with strong financial ratings and low complaint volume. See [Is NYCM a good insurance company?](/qa/is-nycm-a-good-insurance-company)

Essentia Insurance Company — the Markel Corporation subsidiary that exclusively underwrites Hagerty's classic car and collector-vehicle policies. See [Is Essentia Insurance a legitimate company?](/qa/is-essentia-insurance-legit)

Puffin Insurance — a UK direct travel insurance brand whose policies are underwritten by an AXA Group company. See [Is Puffin Travel Insurance legit and worth it?](/qa/is-puffin-travel-insurance-legit)
Amigo Insurance — not one national company, but a name used by several unrelated independent auto insurance agencies. See [Is Amigo Insurance legit?](/qa/is-amigo-insurance-legit)

Insure 90 — a confusing search term that mixes a legacy insurance-agency software product, an insurance coinsurance concept, and unrelated small agencies rather than one identifiable insurer. See [Is Insure 90 a legitimate insurance company?](/qa/is-insure-90-legit)

QuoteLab — a Los Angeles-based insurance lead-generation marketplace, owned by publicly traded MediaAlpha, that connects shoppers with agents rather than selling policies itself. See [What is QuoteLab?](/qa/what-is-quotelab)

Dairyland Insurance — a legitimate, long-established non-standard auto and motorcycle insurer owned by Sentry Insurance Group. See [What is the Dairyland Insurance phone number?](/qa/dairyland-insurance-phone-number)

Allstate — one of the largest US insurers, with an A+ AM Best rating, offering home insurance quotes online, by app, or through an agent. See [How do you get an Allstate home insurance quote?](/qa/allstate-home-insurance-quote)
Amtex Insurance — a family-founded, BBB-accredited independent agency with 85+ locations across Texas. See [Is Amtex Auto Insurance legit?](/qa/amtex-auto-insurance)
Adrian Flux — the UK's largest specialist motor insurance broker, in business since 1973. See [What is My Adrian Flux (MyAccount)?](/qa/my-adrian-flux)

Smart Auto Insurance — not one company, but a generic marketing phrase reused by several unrelated agencies and brands, including a UK motor insurer now administered by AutoProtect (MBI) Ltd. See [Is Smart Auto Insurance legit?](/qa/smart-auto-insurance)

The Responsive Auto Insurance Company — a licensed non-standard auto insurer founded in 2007 and based in Plantation, Florida. See [Is The Responsive Auto Insurance Company legit?](/qa/the-responsive-auto-insurance)
Accusure Insurance — a name shared by at least two unrelated small agencies, and easily confused with the much larger Acrisure. See [Is Accusure Insurance legit?](/qa/accusure-insurance)

Haven Insurance — an active, independent UK motor and home insurer covering 230,000+ policyholders, distinct from an unrelated US agency of the same name. See [What is the Haven Insurance contact number?](/qa/haven-insurance-contact-number)
Erie Insurance — a top-rated (AM Best A+) regional carrier available in just 12 states plus D.C. See [How do you get a quote from Erie Insurance?](/qa/quote-erie-insurance)
Able Insurance Agency — a Carolinas-based independent agency writing auto insurance since 1989. See [Is Able Auto Insurance legit?](/qa/able-auto-insurance)

content.text: What To Do If You Already Bought From an Unfamiliar Name

items: Find the actual underwriting carrier's name on your declarations page — it may differ from the brand you searched for or the agency that sold you the policy, the same way a [Hagerty policy is actually underwritten by Essentia](/qa/is-essentia-insurance-legit) or a [Bamboo-sourced quote is actually underwritten by Sutton National or MS Transverse](/qa/is-bamboo-insurance-admitted-in-california).
Verify that carrier's license and financial strength rating using the steps above, and cross-check reviews via the [Better Business Bureau](https://www.bbb.org/).
Confirm your agent's individual license through the National Insurance Producer Registry (NIPR) or your state's lookup.
Save your state Department of Insurance's consumer complaint contact information in case you ever need to escalate a claims dispute.

If you're evaluating an independent agency itself, rather than the carrier behind it, see [Starting & Running an Insurance Agency](/learn/starting-and-running-an-insurance-agency) for how legitimate agencies are actually licensed and structured.

content.text: This article is for general educational purposes and reflects publicly available information as of the publication date. It is not a recommendation to buy or avoid any specific insurance product, and company details such as ratings, ownership, and licensing status can change. Always confirm current licensing and financial strength ratings directly with your state Department of Insurance, the NAIC, and AM Best before purchasing a policy.
